messages.content: I want to develop long-tail image recognition that preserves rare-class accuracy when predictive background correlations reverse, without using target-domain labels.

The aim is to keep recognition of less common classes reliable even when backgrounds that used to be predictive no longer have the same relationship to the classes. The method must not rely on target-domain labels.
Can we make the performance requirements explicit?

Under background reversals, bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy should improve by at least 5 percentage points over empirical risk minimization. Top-quintile class macro-accuracy should remain within 1 percentage point of that baseline, using identical training data for the comparison.
What does “bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy” emphasize?

It focuses on the average accuracy across classes in the bottom quintile, giving each of those classes equal weight in that group average. In this long-tail setting, that is the rare-class side of the objective; it is not simply overall accuracy across all images.
And the top-quintile requirement is there to keep the frequent classes from paying for the rare-class gain?

Yes. The goal pairs a substantial bottom-quintile improvement with a tight constraint on top-quintile performance relative to empirical risk minimization. It does not call for a rare-class gain at the expense of a large change in the top-quintile macro-accuracy.
Does “within 1 percentage point” mean the top-quintile score cannot drop by more than one point?

It includes that limit, but “within” also bounds a rise: the top-quintile macro-accuracy should differ from the baseline by no more than 1 percentage point in either direction. It is a closeness requirement, rather than a request for a top-quintile improvement.
Could you distinguish percentage points from a percentage increase here?

The thresholds refer to absolute differences between accuracy percentages. For illustration only, if a bottom-quintile macro-accuracy were 40%, a gain of 5 percentage points would bring it to at least 45%; that is not the same as increasing 40% by 5% of its value.
Is the empirical risk minimization comparison meant to use the same training data?

Yes. The top-quintile requirement explicitly calls for comparison with that baseline using identical training data. The stated bottom-quintile improvement is also measured against empirical risk minimization under background reversals; the objective does not describe a gain obtained by adding different training data.
What is meant by a predictive background correlation reversing?

Conceptually, it means a background cue that was predictive of a class in one setting has a reversed association in the setting of interest. The goal concerns recognition under that change, not merely recognition when the original background relationship continues to hold. It does not specify particular backgrounds or classes.
So is the goal specifically about background reversal, rather than every possible distribution shift?
Yes. Predictive background correlations reversing is the condition named here. The statement does not claim the same performance targets for every other kind of shift.
How should I read “without target-domain labels”? Does it specify what other target-domain information is available?
It rules out reliance on target-domain labels. It does not say whether unlabeled target-domain images are available, so that availability should not be assumed either way.
If accuracy is part of the requirement, doesn't someone need labels to measure it?

Measuring an accuracy requires a way to determine whether predictions are correct. That is distinct from giving target-domain labels to the recognition method. The goal sets a no-target-domain-label condition for developing the recognition capability, but it does not spell out an assessment protocol.
Does the five-point target say every rare class must gain five points?

No. It is a requirement on bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy—the group average—not a stated minimum improvement for each individual class. Likewise, the top-quintile condition concerns its group macro-accuracy, not a separate one-point bound for every top-quintile class.
Why specify macro-accuracy for both groups instead of just one overall score?

Separate group macro-accuracies make the two parts of the goal visible: improving performance across the bottom-quintile classes while keeping performance across the top-quintile classes close to the empirical risk minimization baseline. An overall score alone would not express those two requirements.
Am I right that the desired outcome is a target, not an achieved result?
Right. “Develop” states an objective. The 5-percentage-point improvement and the 1-percentage-point top-quintile bound are performance requirements, not reported experimental outcomes.
Does the objective prescribe a particular model or technique for handling backgrounds?

No. It specifies the recognition setting, the absence of target-domain labels, and the two comparisons with empirical risk minimization. It does not prescribe an architecture, training procedure, or background-handling technique.
Let me restate it: improve the bottom quintile under reversed background correlations, but keep the top quintile essentially at the empirical risk minimization level on identical training data.

That captures the balance. More precisely, the bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy must be at least 5 percentage points above empirical risk minimization under background reversals, while top-quintile class macro-accuracy must be within 1 percentage point of that baseline using identical training data. The recognition capability must be developed without target-domain labels.

For that objective, I propose training TailSwap with self-supervised foreground masks, tail-weighted background swaps, and head-class distillation from an empirical risk minimization model trained on the same data.

TailSwap brings together two ideas: use foreground masks to support background swaps that emphasize tail classes, and use the same-data empirical risk minimization model as a distillation reference for head classes. It is a proposed way to pursue the rare-class improvement while guarding head-class performance, not a demonstrated result.
What role do the foreground masks play in the proposal?

They provide a way to distinguish foreground from background for the proposed swaps. Calling them self-supervised specifies how the masks are to be obtained in broad terms, but the proposal does not specify a mask-generation method or claim that the masks are perfect.
Does a background swap mean changing the object the model is supposed to recognize?

The proposal is framed around swapping backgrounds while using foreground masks, so its intended distinction is between the foreground and its surrounding context. It does not specify the exact image transformation or guarantee that a swap leaves every foreground detail untouched.
Why make the swaps tail-weighted?

That weighting directs more of the proposed background-swap emphasis toward tail classes, aligning it with the goal of improving bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy when predictive background correlations reverse. The proposal does not give a numerical weighting rule or a swap frequency.
So we are not saying that only tail-class images receive swaps?
Correct. “Tail-weighted” conveys greater emphasis on the tail; it does not, by itself, say that swaps are exclusive to tail classes.
How does head-class distillation fit with that emphasis?

It adds a head-class preservation component. The proposal uses an empirical risk minimization model trained on the same data as the distillation reference for head classes, alongside the tail-weighted swaps. That pairing reflects the goal of improving the bottom quintile without letting top-quintile class macro-accuracy stray far from the baseline, though it does not establish that either threshold will be met.
When you say “distillation,” are you specifying a particular loss?

No. Distillation here identifies guidance from the same-data empirical risk minimization model for head classes. The proposal does not specify its loss function, how strongly that guidance is weighted, or other training details.
Is the empirical risk minimization model a separate source of training data?
No additional training data is specified. “Same-data ERM” identifies an empirical risk minimization reference trained on the same data, consistent with the goal's identical-training-data comparison.
Does self-supervision for the masks imply we can use labeled target-domain examples?

No. The objective remains to develop recognition without target-domain labels. Self-supervised foreground masks are part of the proposed training approach; they do not introduce an exception to that condition.
Do we know where the backgrounds used for swaps come from?
The proposal does not say. It specifies tail-weighted background swaps supported by self-supervised foreground masks, but not a source-selection procedure for the backgrounds.
Would it be accurate to say TailSwap has already made the model robust to reversed correlations?

No. TailSwap is a training proposal. The background swaps are intended to address reliance on predictive backgrounds when those correlations reverse, but the proposal does not report a measured robustness gain.
And does head-class distillation ensure the one-point condition?

It is proposed to help preserve head-class behavior relative to the same-data empirical risk minimization reference. It is not a guarantee that top-quintile class macro-accuracy will remain within 1 percentage point of the baseline; that remains a performance requirement.
Could you distinguish the two parts without turning them into separate methods?

Within TailSwap, tail-weighted background swaps are the part aimed at reducing dependence on backgrounds for less common classes. Head-class distillation from same-data ERM is the part aimed at retaining head-class performance. Both are components of the single proposed training approach.
Does this proposal change the numerical targets we discussed?

No. The objective remains an improvement of 5 percentage points in bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy over empirical risk minimization under background reversals, with top-quintile class macro-accuracy within 1 percentage point of that baseline using identical training data. TailSwap proposes an approach to those targets without claiming to have achieved them.
How much foreground-mask error can TailSwap tolerate before background swaps erase discriminative rare-class features?

There is no stated numerical tolerance. The concern is that a mask might treat part of a rare-class foreground as background, allowing a swap to replace a feature the recognition model needs. How much error is tolerable would depend on which parts are misidentified, not just how many pixels the mask gets wrong.
So an overall mask-error percentage would not answer the question on its own?

Right. The same percentage of error could fall on relatively unimportant regions or on a small, highly discriminative part of the foreground. The question is about whether the swap damages useful rare-class information, rather than mask accuracy in the abstract.
Which direction of mask error is the direct danger here?

If the mask incorrectly marks foreground as background, a background swap could alter or remove that foreground content. Marking background as foreground is a different error: it could leave some background in place, but it does not by itself describe the erasure of a foreground feature.
Would any foreground pixel marked as background mean the swap has gone too far?

Not necessarily. The question turns on whether the affected content is discriminative for the rare class. A mask error touching foreground is a warning about possible damage; it is not, by itself, proof that a class-defining feature has been erased.
When I say “erase,” should I mean that the feature literally disappears from a swapped image?

That is one possible meaning. It could also refer more broadly to the swap making the feature unavailable or unreliable as a cue for recognition. The question does not specify a precise definition of erasure, so neither interpretation supplies a numerical cutoff.
Can we at least say that smaller mask errors are always safer?

Not as an absolute rule. A small error in a crucial part of a rare-class foreground could matter more than a larger error elsewhere. Error size is relevant, but its location and what the affected region conveys are relevant too.
Is this risk particular to the tail-weighted part of TailSwap?

Tail-weighting makes the concern especially pertinent to rare classes: those are the classes emphasized by the proposed background swaps. But the underlying issue—foreground mistakenly included in a background change—does not depend on a particular numerical weighting.
Does having self-supervised foreground masks tell us how much error they will have?
No. “Self-supervised” describes the proposed way of obtaining the masks in broad terms. It gives neither a mask-error rate nor a bound on errors affecting discriminative foreground regions.
What if a mask preserves most of an object but misses a distinctive detail?

That captures the core concern. Preserving most of the foreground by area would not settle whether a missed detail matters for recognizing the rare class. If a swap changes that detail, the apparent size of the mask error could understate its significance.
And if a mask includes some background as foreground?

Then a proposed background swap might leave some original context intact. That may matter to the aim of reducing reliance on background correlations, but it is distinct from the specific question of swaps erasing discriminative rare-class features.
Could I frame tolerance as the point where errors begin to hurt rare-class recognition?

You can frame it that way conceptually, provided “begin to hurt” is not treated as an already known threshold. The question asks where mask errors become consequential for rare-class features and recognition; it does not establish that point or say it is the same across all rare classes.
Does the same-data empirical risk minimization reference tell us the mask-error tolerance?

No. It identifies a reference for comparison and, in the TailSwap proposal, head-class distillation. Neither role specifies how much foreground-mask error the background swaps can tolerate without damaging rare-class cues.
I don't want to imply that the swaps definitely erase features whenever the masks are imperfect.

Then the conditional wording is important: foreground-mask errors *could* cause a swap to alter discriminative rare-class content when the errors overlap that content. The open question is how much such error TailSwap can tolerate before that risk becomes consequential; no tolerance value or observed outcome has been stated.

Here is a hypothesis about mask-error tolerance: under reversed backgrounds, TailSwap gains at least 5 tail-accuracy percentage points versus ERM without more than a 1-percentage-point head-accuracy loss, provided the foreground-mask false-negative rate is at most 10%.

That states a conditional hypothesis, not a measured result. It proposes that, when the foreground-mask false-negative rate is 10% or lower, TailSwap achieves both the tail gain and the limit on head loss relative to empirical risk minimization (ERM) under reversed backgrounds.
How does the 10% condition relate to my question about swaps erasing rare-class features?

A foreground-mask false negative is foreground incorrectly treated as background, making that content vulnerable to a background swap. The hypothesis proposes that TailSwap can still deliver the stated tail and head accuracy outcomes when that error rate is no greater than 10%. It does not claim that no discriminative rare-class feature is ever affected.
Is 10% supposed to be the amount of the foreground that a swap actually erases?

No. A false-negative rate concerns foreground the mask fails to identify; it is not, by itself, a measurement of features erased by the resulting swaps. A mask error may create an opportunity to alter foreground content, but the hypothesis does not quantify how much discriminative content a swap changes.
What does the “at most” sign include?
It includes a foreground-mask false-negative rate of exactly 10%, as well as rates below 10%. The hypothesis makes no prediction for rates above 10%.
Does that mean TailSwap fails as soon as the rate exceeds 10%?
No. The condition marks the range covered by this hypothesis. It neither establishes failure above 10% nor identifies 10% as a sharp failure boundary.
And does it say the condition is necessary for a five-point tail gain?
No. It proposes the performance outcome when the false-negative rate is no greater than 10%; it does not say a rate above 10% makes the outcome impossible.
Could a mask meet the 10% rate and still miss an especially important rare-class detail?

Yes. An aggregate false-negative rate does not specify where the missed foreground lies. Even within the proposed limit, an error could touch a discriminative detail. That is why the accuracy claim remains a hypothesis rather than a guarantee derived from the mask percentage alone.
Am I constraining all kinds of mask error to 10%?

No. The condition specifically concerns foreground-mask false negatives—true foreground missed by the mask. It does not state a bound on false positives, where background is incorrectly included as foreground, or on an overall mask-error rate.
What exactly is the tail comparison?

Under reversed backgrounds, the hypothesized TailSwap tail accuracy is at least 5 percentage points higher than ERM tail accuracy. The long-tail objective frames the tail measure as bottom-quintile class macro-accuracy; the hypothesis states a five-point tail-accuracy gain rather than a five-percent relative increase.
Does that require every tail class to improve by five points?
No. The stated gain is for tail accuracy as a group measure in this context, not a promise of a five-percentage-point improvement for each individual tail class.
Please unpack “without more than a 1-point head loss.”

Relative to ERM, TailSwap's head accuracy must not be lower by more than 1 percentage point under the hypothesized conditions. A loss of exactly 1 percentage point is permitted by that wording. It does not specify a separate upper bound on a head-accuracy gain.
Is that identical to saying head accuracy is within 1 percentage point of ERM?

Not quite. “Within 1 percentage point” limits differences in either direction, while “without more than a 1-point head loss” limits the downward difference. This hypothesis states the head-loss condition; it does not itself constrain an improvement of more than 1 percentage point.
Are both accuracy comparisons under the background reversal?

Yes. “Under reversed backgrounds” conditions the hypothesized tail gain versus ERM and the limit on head loss. The statement is not a claim about TailSwap's performance under every possible background relationship.
Does this hypothesis imply we have established that the masks reach 10% false negatives?

No. It neither reports a measured mask false-negative rate nor establishes the proposed accuracy outcomes. The rate is a condition in the hypothesis, not an observed property of the self-supervised masks.
And it does not change the proposal to use tail-weighted background swaps and same-data ERM head-class distillation?

Correct. It is a performance hypothesis about TailSwap under a specified foreground-mask error condition. It does not add a training mechanism or change the proposed tail-weighted background swaps and head-class distillation from same-data ERM.

So the careful phrasing is that TailSwap may tolerate up to 10% foreground-mask false negatives while achieving those two accuracy comparisons—not that 10% is a proven safe level for every rare-class feature?

Exactly. The hypothesis predicts at least a 5-percentage-point tail-accuracy gain versus ERM and no greater than a 1-percentage-point head-accuracy loss under reversed backgrounds when the foreground-mask false-negative rate is at most 10%. Whether that prediction holds, and what happens to particular discriminative features, are not established by the hypothesis.

To investigate how much mask error TailSwap can tolerate, I want to sweep foreground-mask false negatives from 0% to 30% during TailSwap training, then compare tail and head macro-accuracy under reversed backgrounds with same-data ERM.

That is a plan to vary the foreground-mask false-negative rate across the 0–30% range during TailSwap training and examine both tail and head class macro-accuracy under reversed backgrounds. Same-data empirical risk minimization (ERM) is the comparison baseline. The plan does not yet state any results or a maximum tolerable error rate.
Why focus the sweep on false negatives rather than mask error generally?

A foreground-mask false negative is foreground that the mask treats as background. In TailSwap, that is the error direction most directly connected to the concern that a background swap might alter discriminative rare-class content. The sweep does not, by itself, cover every kind of mask error.
Does a 30% false-negative setting mean that 30% of rare-class features have been erased?

No. It describes a foreground-mask error rate during training, not a measured rate of feature erasure. Whether the missed foreground contains discriminative features, and whether a swap actually removes their usefulness, are separate questions.
What should I take the 0% end of the sweep to mean?

It is the end of the planned range with no foreground-mask false negatives. That does not, on its own, say the masks have no other errors or that recognition under reversed backgrounds will be perfect.
And the 30% end is simply the upper end we plan to examine?
Yes. The plan covers foreground-mask false-negative rates from 0% through 30%. It does not say that 30% is tolerable, that TailSwap fails there, or that the same behavior continues beyond that range.
Does “sweep” commit us to checking every whole-number percentage between the endpoints?
No. It specifies the range to vary during TailSwap training, but not the spacing or number of settings within that range. Those details are not stated in the plan.
Am I varying the masks during training or just sorting an evaluation afterward by mask quality?

The plan says to sweep the false-negative rates during TailSwap training. The comparison afterward is of tail and head macro-accuracy under reversed backgrounds against same-data ERM. It does not describe merely sorting a fixed model's evaluation results.
Does the plan specify how those false-negative rates are produced?
No. It identifies the error dimension and the 0–30% training sweep, but not a procedure for obtaining each mask-error setting.
Why compare both tail and head macro-accuracy rather than only rare-class accuracy?

Both sides matter to the long-tail recognition objective. Tail macro-accuracy shows how the less common classes fare as the mask false-negative rate varies, while head macro-accuracy shows whether performance for the more common classes changes relative to ERM. The plan calls for both comparisons under reversed backgrounds.
What does macro-accuracy add to those comparisons?

It makes the comparison about accuracy averaged across classes within each group, rather than an accuracy that gives more weight to classes simply because they have more images. The plan examines that group-level measure separately for the tail and the head.
Is the baseline supposed to use different training data for each comparison?
No. The stated comparison is with same-data ERM. The plan does not specify additional data for the baseline or say how many baseline models to train.
Does the ERM model itself undergo the mask-error sweep?
The sweep is specified for TailSwap training. ERM is named as the same-data comparison baseline; the plan does not say to apply the foreground-mask false-negative sweep to ERM.
Why make the accuracy comparison under reversed backgrounds specifically?

That is the condition in which the background correlations of interest have reversed. Comparing tail and head macro-accuracy there keeps the assessment focused on the setting the plan names, rather than assuming results in an unchanged-background setting would answer the same question.
If TailSwap's tail macro-accuracy changes across the sweep, would that prove a swap erased rare-class features?

Not by itself. A change in macro-accuracy would show a performance difference associated with the training settings in the sweep. The accuracy comparison alone would not identify which image features a swap altered or establish that a particular rare-class feature was erased.
So what can this plan say about mask-error tolerance?

It can examine how TailSwap's tail and head macro-accuracies under reversed backgrounds compare with same-data ERM across the planned false-negative range. That would make performance sensitivity to this kind of mask error visible. The plan alone does not supply the outcomes or a numerical tolerance boundary.
Should I describe the sweep as covering all possible ways a mask could be wrong?
No. It varies foreground-mask false negatives from 0% to 30%. It does not specify a sweep of false positives, an overall mask-error rate, or every possible placement of errors within the foreground.
Is the location of a missed foreground region relevant even if two settings have the same false-negative rate?

Potentially. The same rate can describe errors in different foreground locations, and those locations may differ in importance for recognition. The plan specifies rates to sweep, not how errors at a given rate are distributed across foreground regions.
I want to keep the description as a plan, not imply that the comparison has already identified a safe rate.

Then state it prospectively: sweep 0–30% foreground-mask false negatives during TailSwap training and compare reversed-background tail and head macro-accuracy with same-data ERM. Whether any setting preserves discriminative rare-class information or meets a desired performance level remains to be determined.
Let's make the mask-error sweep concrete: run it on LT-CUB-Rev at 0%, 5%, 10%, 20%, and 30%, then compare TailSwap's tail and head macro-accuracy under reversed backgrounds with same-data ERM.

The activity is to run TailSwap at those five foreground-mask false-negative settings and make the tail and head macro-accuracy comparisons under reversed backgrounds. Same-data empirical risk minimization (ERM) is the reference. This specifies what to run and compare, not results from a completed sweep.
Are those percentages accuracy targets or mask-error settings?

They are foreground-mask false-negative settings for the TailSwap sweep: 0%, 5%, 10%, 20%, and 30%. Tail and head macro-accuracy are the outcomes to compare with ERM; the listed percentages are not those accuracy outcomes.
Which of those settings bear directly on the hypothesis about a false-negative rate of at most 10%?

The 0%, 5%, and 10% settings fall within that condition, including its 10% boundary. The 20% and 30% settings extend the sweep beyond it. Results at the first three settings could be compared with the hypothesized gain of at least 5 tail-accuracy percentage points versus ERM without more than a 1-percentage-point head-accuracy loss, under reversed backgrounds.
Should I treat 20% and 30% as predicted failures?
No. The hypothesis does not make a prediction above 10%. Including 20% and 30% lets the activity examine TailSwap's performance there, without presuming either success or failure.
Does 0% mean the masks are entirely correct?
It means no foreground-mask false negatives at that setting. It does not rule out other mask errors, such as background mistakenly marked as foreground.
Where does the background reversal enter the activity?

It is the condition for the tail and head macro-accuracy comparison. The sweep varies foreground-mask false negatives during TailSwap training; the stated performance comparison is TailSwap versus same-data ERM under reversed backgrounds.
Are we comparing one overall accuracy number for TailSwap with ERM?
No. The activity calls for separate tail and head macro-accuracy comparisons. That keeps the rare-class side and the frequent-class side visible rather than combining them into one overall score.
Does same-data ERM undergo the five mask-error settings too?
The five settings are specified for the TailSwap mask-error sweep. ERM is the same-data comparison reference; this activity does not specify applying those mask-error settings to ERM.
What would a difference of five points mean in this comparison?

It would mean a difference of five percentage points between the compared tail macro-accuracies—not a five-percent relative change and not a five-point gain for every individual tail class. No such difference has been reported here.
Can the head comparison alone tell us whether foreground features were erased?

No. Head macro-accuracy indicates how head-class recognition compares with ERM. Even a change in tail macro-accuracy would not, by itself, show that a particular rare-class feature was erased by a swap. The activity measures performance across mask-error settings; it does not specify a direct inspection of altered features.
Does naming LT-CUB-Rev tell us anything else about the data or how reversals were constructed?
Not from this activity description. LT-CUB-Rev identifies where to run the sweep, but no additional details about its construction or the reversal procedure are specified.
So how should I describe this without implying we already know TailSwap's tolerance?

Say that the LT-CUB-Rev activity will run TailSwap with foreground-mask false-negative settings of 0%, 5%, 10%, 20%, and 30%, and compare its reversed-background tail and head macro-accuracy with same-data ERM. Those comparisons are intended to examine sensitivity to mask error, including the settings covered by the at-most-10% hypothesis; they have not yet established a tolerable error level.

The LT-CUB-Rev sweep now has results to discuss. Under reversed backgrounds, at 10% foreground-mask misses, TailSwap reached 43.1% tail macro-accuracy and 81.5% head macro-accuracy. Same-data ERM was at 37.8% and 82.1%, respectively. At 20% mask misses, TailSwap's tail macro-accuracy fell to 41.0%.

At the 10% mask-miss setting, TailSwap's tail macro-accuracy was 5.3 percentage points above same-data ERM: 43.1% versus 37.8%. Its head macro-accuracy was 0.6 percentage points below ERM: 81.5% versus 82.1%. The reported 20% result is a TailSwap tail macro-accuracy of 41.0%, down 2.1 percentage points from its 10% result.
Are those percentage-point differences, rather than relative percentage changes?
Yes. They are direct differences between accuracy percentages. For example, 43.1% minus 37.8% is 5.3 percentage points; it is not a 5.3% relative increase.
At 20% mask misses, how does the reported tail number compare with ERM?

TailSwap's reported tail macro-accuracy at 20% was 41.0%, which is 3.2 percentage points above ERM's reported 37.8% tail macro-accuracy. It is also 2.1 percentage points below TailSwap's 43.1% at 10% mask misses.
Do we have a head macro-accuracy number for TailSwap at 20%?
No head macro-accuracy at 20% is included in these reported results. The 20% observation gives only TailSwap's tail macro-accuracy, so it cannot establish a head-accuracy comparison at that setting.
Can I say that the larger mask-miss setting erased discriminative rare-class features?

Not from these accuracy numbers alone. The tail macro-accuracy fell from 43.1% at 10% misses to 41.0% at 20%, but that performance difference does not identify which foreground features were altered or show that any particular feature was erased.
Is the 10% miss rate a percentage of images that had bad masks?
That is not what is stated. It is the foreground-mask miss, or false-negative, rate used for the setting. The reported results do not express it as a percentage of images with any mask error.
What is the narrowest accurate description of the head result?

At 10% foreground-mask misses on LT-CUB-Rev under reversed backgrounds, TailSwap's head macro-accuracy was 81.5%, compared with 82.1% for same-data ERM—a 0.6-percentage-point lower score. The figures given here do not describe head performance at the other mask-miss settings.
And the tail result at that same setting?
At 10% foreground-mask misses, TailSwap's reversed-background tail macro-accuracy was 43.1%, compared with 37.8% for same-data ERM—a 5.3-percentage-point higher score.
We ran a sweep with other settings too. Should I fill in the 0%, 5%, or 30% values when describing these results?

No. Although those settings were part of the LT-CUB-Rev sweep, the results stated here give TailSwap tail and head macro-accuracy at 10%, plus TailSwap tail macro-accuracy at 20%. They do not provide numerical outcomes for 0%, 5%, or 30%.
Does the fall to 41.0% establish that 10% is the exact maximum mask-miss rate TailSwap can tolerate?

No. It shows a lower reported tail macro-accuracy at the 20% setting than at the 10% setting. These figures do not establish an exact tolerance boundary or describe performance at every rate between those settings.
Then let's keep the result statement limited to the measured comparisons.

On LT-CUB-Rev under reversed backgrounds, TailSwap at 10% foreground-mask misses recorded 43.1% tail and 81.5% head macro-accuracy, versus 37.8% and 82.1% for same-data ERM. At 20% misses, TailSwap's reported tail macro-accuracy was 41.0%. No head result at 20% or direct measurement of feature erasure is stated.
Let's advance TailSwap only with foreground-mask false-negative rates of 10% or less. At 20% errors, the tail gain drops below five points.

That sets a condition for advancing TailSwap: foreground-mask false negatives must be at most 10%. The stated reason is that, at the 20% setting, the tail-accuracy gain over ERM under reversed backgrounds is less than the five-percentage-point target.
Does “at most 10%” include exactly 10%?
Yes. A foreground-mask false-negative rate of exactly 10% meets the decision's condition; a rate above 10% does not.
Am I setting a limit on every kind of mask error?
No. The limit specifically concerns foreground-mask false negatives: foreground that the mask misses. It does not state a limit on false positives or on overall mask error.
Does the decision mean TailSwap fails at every rate above 10%?

No. It says to advance TailSwap only at rates of 10% or less, and gives the below-five-point tail gain at 20% as the reason. It does not report results for every rate above 10% or claim that all such rates have the same outcome.
Should I describe 10% as an exact failure boundary?
No. It is the cutoff in this advancement decision, not an established point at which performance abruptly changes. The stated performance concern is at 20% errors.
When I say the gain falls below five points, what is it being compared against?

The tail-accuracy gain is relative to the same-data empirical risk minimization baseline under reversed backgrounds. “Below five points” means less than a five-percentage-point advantage over that baseline, not a tail accuracy below 5%.
Does a gain below five points mean there is no gain at all?
No. It means the gain does not reach five percentage points. That wording alone does not say the gain is zero or negative.
Is the 20% result the only reason stated for this decision?
Yes. The decision explicitly gives the reduced tail gain at 20% foreground-mask errors as its reason for limiting advancement to rates of 10% or less. It does not add another reason.
Are we concluding anything about head-class accuracy at 20%?
No. The stated reason concerns the tail gain falling below five points at 20%. This decision does not make a head-accuracy claim for that error setting.
Does satisfying the mask-rate condition automatically prove TailSwap meets both accuracy requirements?

No. The rate is a condition for advancing TailSwap, not a guarantee about its accuracy. The decision should not be read as proving a five-point tail gain or a particular head-class result at every rate of 10% or less.
I also don't want “advance” to sound like we have specified a new training procedure.
